selfReportForSkill.note: Self-report is invalid for skill diagnosis (Dunning-Kruger); diagnose behaviourally.

selfReportForConstraints.note: Self-report remains valid for constraints/goals/resources — not a skill claim.

instantEvalGames.note: Client-side instant-analysis budget at onboarding; consumed in M5.

minItems.note: IRT ladder length lower bound; best-guess.

maxItems.note: IRT ladder length upper bound; best-guess.

timeBudgetMin.note: ≈3 min keeps onboarding cognitive load low; exact length best-guess.

startRating.note: Default ladder start when the user has no platform rating.

targetSuccessRate.note: Servo target; pattern-learning sweet spot ≈85%, conservative 80%.

stepUp.note: Transformed staircase: raise difficulty by this much after a solve.

stepDown.note: 4× stepUp ⇒ ladder converges to ~80% success (the target above).

ratingFloor.note: Lower clamp of the calibration rating span.

ratingCeil.note: Upper clamp of the calibration rating span.

abilitySpread.note: Maps (success − target) to a rating offset in the estimator.

uncertaintyBase.note: Estimate SE at n=1; shrinks by √n as items accrue.

stopUncertainty.note: Stop the ladder early once SE drops below this (and minItems met).

blunderCpLoss.note: A move losing ≥150cp (from the mover's perspective) is a blunder.

excludeDecidedAboveCp.note: Ignore blunders in already-decided positions (|eval| already > 600cp).

blunderWinProbDrop.note: Win-probability drop (~150cp near equality) that marks a blunder — mate-safe: a missed mate that stays winning is a ~0 drop, so it never inflates the blunder rate.

u800.note: Expected blunder rate; reports disagree — recalibrate from telemetry.

weaknessMultiplier.note: Flag a weakness when the user's rate exceeds 1.2× the band baseline.

low.note: ≥20 trailing games to flag a blunder-rate weakness at all (binomial power).

estMinutes.note: Time-budget estimate for packing; not a chess value.
Time-budget estimate only; the rich book interaction (recommendations, the active-recall/85%/Woodpecker protocol, and logging) lives on the /library surface.

delivery.note: Books stay EXTERNAL — recommended + logged, never hosted (VISION §6).

u800.note: The conservative stub keeps book study on the dedicated /library surface rather than forcing it into the timed daily mix (daily-mix ROI prior 0); the research config can raise this with no Engine change.

successTarget.note: Productive-struggle target for the calculation track (50–60%).

controllerSuccessToRating.note: Servo gain: a success-rate error maps to this many rating points of offset nudge.

beginnerSuccessTarget.note: Motivational override for the fragile early phase; a motivation, not learning-rate, choice.

motifMasteryThreshold.note: Block a new motif until accuracy clears this, then interleave it.

workedExampleComplexityThreshold.note: Show a worked example before active testing at high element-interactivity.

ratingFloor.note: Lower clamp for any servo-produced puzzle-rating target.

ratingCeil.note: Upper clamp for any servo-produced puzzle-rating target.

desiredRetention.note: FSRS desired retention; 0.90 default (validated on flashcards; chess-spatial validity unverified).

maximumIntervalDays.note: Interval cap (days) — an infra sanity bound, not a learning value.

fsrsWeights.note: FSRS-6 default 21-weight vector (Anki corpus); personalise from telemetry after ~1000 reviews.

fastFactor.note: Correct & solve time < band-median × 0.5 → Easy (FSRS grade 4).

slowFactor.note: Correct & solve time > band-median × 1.5 → Hard (2); between → Good (3).

intraSessionRetestDelaySec.note: Within-session wait (10 min) before a just-failed puzzle is retested without its hint (§7.5 redo flow). The exact gap is unstudied; a short delay beats an immediate massed retest.

weaknessSeverity.note: Weight on a current weakness signal (A descriptive / C as a training prescription).

formatMismatchPenalty.note: Down-weight a format-specific activity the user never plays; magnitude best-guess.

ownedResourceBonus.note: Prefer a resource the user already owns; magnitude best-guess.

depthWeaknessBonus.note: Depth preference concentrates on the biggest weakness; magnitude best-guess.

breadthRoiBonus.note: Breadth preference spreads across high-ROI activities; magnitude best-guess.

dailyPuzzleDose.note: A CAP, not a fixed count: the session fits the hard time budget and stops at min(this, time available). Deliberately no volume-chasing (S7).

pattern.note: Pattern-recognition puzzles are quick (~45s each); the time cap bounds how many fit.

calculation.note: Deep calculation/visualisation puzzles need longer (~3 min each).

dailyChoiceCount.note: SDT autonomy: offer a few science-backed paths/day; the count is best-guess.

freeSkipsPerWeek.note: Allow skipping one module/week with no penalty (autonomy support).

streakCapDays.note: Streak resets to a fresh cycle each week — capped, never infinite (anti-loss-aversion); the number is best-guess.

consistencyWindowDays.note: Track consistency asymptotically over ~90 days, not as an unbroken streak.

habitExpectationDays.note: Median time to automate a habit (range 18–254); communicate honestly, don't promise.

competenceMilestones.note: Badge thresholds for genuine work (e.g. 'completed 100 reviews'); the exact counts are arbitrary.

peerComparison.note: Same-level anonymised peer comparison is opt-in; shipped OFF in the stub (conservative).

globalLeaderboards.note: FORBIDDEN: global leaderboards drive downward social comparison and backfire (dark pattern).

reminderCadenceCapPerDay.note: Anti-nag ceiling: at most one reminder/day, user-configurable; the number is best-guess.

tiltCooldownLossStreak.note: Suggest a break after this many consecutive losses; thin chess evidence — forgiving default only.

rdBaselineMax.note: Use a rating as a baseline only when RD ≤ this (enough recent games); the threshold value is best-guess.

plateauWindowDays.note: Flag a plateau when the CI upper bound sets no new high over this many active days; the CI-crossing rule is evidenced, the window best-guess.

physicalBoardRecommendation.value: advise for bands >1200 preparing for OTB

rationale.whenShown: a solving board with hidden interface crutches
rationale.value: Over-the-board play doesn't let you hover pieces or draw arrows. Hiding these crutches makes you hold the variation in your head, which is what builds calculation and visualisation.

rationale.whenShown: a personalised blunder drill in the daily session
rationale.value: These are the exact positions where you blundered in your own games — re-solving them, spaced over days, is the most science-backed way to stop repeating a mistake. The spacing effect is strong in general learning; its use on whole chess positions is our own extrapolation, not proven.

rationale.whenShown: the within-session wait before retesting a just-failed puzzle
rationale.value: We wait a little before showing this puzzle again, without its hint. An immediate retest only checks your short-term memory; a short gap forces a real recall and makes the pattern stick. The ideal gap length isn't settled, so this is a best guess.
Below master level, games are usually decided by the last blunder. Today targets board safety.
Playing full-length games is the strongest single correlate of rating in the data. That's correlation, not proof — but it's where real skill is tested.
You learn fastest at around 80–85% success: hard enough to make you think, easy enough to lock in the pattern.
Re-solving your misses, spaced over days, is the most science-backed way to make patterns stick — proven mostly on flashcards, not chess yet.

Analysing your own games is the single strongest vehicle for building pattern recognition — but how you analyse matters enormously. We guide you through a science-backed process: think first, engine second.
A few key endgame positions turn draws into wins. They matter more as you climb.
Slow, calculate-to-the-end puzzles train depth. Aim for ~50–60% success — these are meant to be hard.
Mixed themes feel harder, and that's the point — in a real game nobody tells you what to look for.
A little most days beats cramming — one of the most reliable findings in learning science. We keep sessions short so fatigue doesn't wreck accuracy.
Your goal today is what you can control — finishing these reps — not your rating. Research on athletes shows process goals beat outcome goals for results and confidence.
We can't promise a rating. No training activity is proven to cause rating gains, and how much people improve varies enormously. We personalise to your trajectory and show our evidence.
Climbing 100 points takes a month or two near 1000, but often years around 1800 — that's normal, not you stalling. We measure you against your own past, never an average.
We re-estimate each skill from your logged results. Early estimates are rough — we show them with their uncertainty, never as a verdict.

Your rating hasn't cleared its noise band in a while. At your level that's statistically normal — the fix is changing the stimulus (harder sweet-spot puzzles, your recurring mistakes), not just doing more.
You've trained another day. We cap the streak at a week on purpose and reset it gently — consistency over weeks is what counts, and one missed day never wipes your progress.
Milestone reached. These badges mark genuine work you've put in — never just time spent or money paid — because rewards tied to an already-interesting task can quietly sap the motivation to do it.

You didn't lose your progress for missing a day. A habit takes on the order of two months to automate, and one skipped day barely dents that — punitive streak-resets mostly just make people quit. Pick it back up today.
This grid shows your effort over time, not a fragile streak. Aim to fill in most days — perfect attendance isn't the goal, and the long view is what builds a habit.

The engine is off on purpose. Turning it on first is like reading the answer key before trying the problem — you recognise the answer but don't learn the method. By thinking first, you train the exact brain pathways you need during your next game.
We filter the computer's suggestions. A move that only makes sense 15 moves deep doesn't help your game now. We focus on the mistakes you can understand and avoid next time.

We don't require the engine's literal top move. Any alternative that recovers most of what you lost, and stays inside this level's visibility threshold, counts as correct — practical chess usually has more than one right answer.

People learn more easily and with more enjoyment from their successes. Analysis of millions of online games shows that sharpening games you played well produces more rating improvement than constantly staring at painful losses.

Emotions cloud your judgement after a game. By pausing briefly, you prevent yourself from ignoring mistakes out of frustration. Research shows that players who tilt process their own errors worse neurologically.

Tomorrow you'll have forgotten 40% of what you learned today. By replaying your own mistakes as puzzles just before you'd forget them, we move the pattern permanently into long-term memory. This is how intuition is built.

This position is chaotic — even the engine gives several nearly-equal options. We're flagging it so you know: this isn't a clear mistake, it's a genuinely complex situation where multiple moves were reasonable.

Cover the page and guess the moves before you read on. Passive reading feels smooth but builds little lasting memory; actively retrieving the move trains the exact pathways you use in a game. (Strong in general learning; the chess-specific transfer is our extrapolation.)

rationale.whenShown: logging a book session's success rate
rationale.value: We aim for roughly a 15% miss rate. If a book feels too easy or too hard, your brain stops learning efficiently — tell us how the exercises went and we'll nudge the difficulty.

Re-solving the same set with a shrinking time limit moves patterns from slow calculation to fast recognition. We space the cycles out rather than cramming them. (Builds fluency; not proven to raise rating.)
If you play over the board, you need physical-board practice. Screens are faster for learning basic patterns, but a real board trains the 3D vision that prevents over-the-board blind spots.

Rehearsing tournament conditions — a physical board, no arrows, writing your moves, strict touch-move — inoculates you against over-the-board stress. Online play without that pressure shows nearly 17% more error.
